options: It throws, because a slice is read-only
questions.explanation: A span is just a view (pointer plus length) over the same memory, so `middle[0]` is `numbers[1]` and writing to it changes the original array.

questions.prompt: When is inserting into the middle of a `LinkedList<T>` an O(1) operation?
options: Always, because linked lists never shift elements
Only when you already hold the node reference, for example from an earlier `Find`
Only when the list has fewer than 16 elements
Only when you insert by position with an index
questions.explanation: The insert itself is O(1), but reaching the position means walking the list, which is O(n). It is O(1) overall only when you already hold the `LinkedListNode<T>`.

questions.prompt: You need a max-heap, but .NET's `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>` is a min-heap by default. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Enqueue each item with its priority negated
Call `Dequeue` twice to skip the smallest item
Use `SortedSet<T>` instead, because it allows duplicates
questions.explanation: `Dequeue` returns the minimum-priority item, so negating the priority (`pq.Enqueue(item, -priority)`) makes the largest value come out first.

questions.prompt: You need a sorted collection that can hold duplicate values. Why isn't `SortedSet<T>` enough on its own, and what can you use instead?
options: It only sorts strings; use `SortedList<TKey, TValue>` instead
It is O(n) per insert; use `List<T>` and call `Sort()` after every add
It disallows duplicates; use a `SortedDictionary<T, int>` that maps each value to its count
It is unordered; use `HashSet<T>` to keep the order
questions.explanation: `SortedSet<T>` disallows duplicates. The lesson suggests pairing the value with a tiebreaker, or using `SortedDictionary<T, int>` as a multiset (value → count).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `List<T>.RemoveAt(index)` and `List<T>.Remove(value)`?
options: `RemoveAt` removes every element equal to the value; `Remove` removes one element by index
`RemoveAt` removes by index; `Remove` searches for the value and removes only its first match
`RemoveAt` returns `true` or `false`; `Remove` throws when the value is missing
They are the same method under two names
questions.explanation: `RemoveAt` removes by index and shifts the later elements; `Remove` searches by value, removes only the first match and returns `true` if it removed something.
